title: He sold 10% of Apple for $800. Was it a mistake?
summary: Ronald Wayne walked away from Apple after 12 days. Hindsight says disaster. What he knew at the time says something else.
body: In April 1976, Ronald Wayne co-founded Apple with Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak. He held 10% of the new partnership, wrote its partnership agreement and drew the company's first logo.
Twelve days later, he gave up his stake for $800.

The internet calls it the worst decision in history. But look at what he knew at the time. Jobs had borrowed money to fill Apple's first big order, about $15,000. In a general partnership, each partner can be personally liable for the business's debts. Wayne was older than his partners and owned a house and a car. They had far less to lose. If Apple failed, creditors could come after what he owned.
Asked about it again in 2026, Wayne said he has no regrets.
lesson: A decision can be sensible and still turn out badly. Judge it by what was known at the time, not by how it ended.
check_title: Before any partnership, loan or guarantee, ask:
check: If this goes wrong, what can they take from me personally?

title: Do 70% of lottery winners really go broke?
summary: It's one of the most-shared money stats online. We looked for the study behind it and couldn't find one.
body: "Seventy percent of lottery winners go broke." You've probably heard it. We went looking for the study behind it, and couldn't find one.
The figure is usually credited to the US National Endowment for Financial Education (NEFE). In 2018, NEFE said the statistic is not backed by its research.

So what does research actually show? A study of almost 35,000 Florida lottery winners compared people who won $50,000 to $150,000 with people who won under $10,000. The bigger winners were less likely to file for bankruptcy right after winning, but about 50 percent more likely to file three to five years later. The money delayed bankruptcy. It didn't prevent it.
In Sweden, researchers following large lottery winners found they reported higher life satisfaction for more than a decade after winning.
lesson: Sudden money doesn't fix money habits. If a windfall lands on you, slow down before any big decision.

title: Is the 10,000-hour rule true?
summary: Practise 10,000 hours and you'll be world-class. The scientist behind the original study said that's not what he found.
body: A 2008 bestseller made it famous: practise for 10,000 hours and you'll be world-class at anything.

But in the original 1993 study by Anders Ericsson and colleagues, 10,000 hours was an average, for the best violinists by age 20. It wasn't a threshold, and plenty of them had practised less. Ericsson later wrote that the popular rule misread his work.

In 2014, a review of 88 studies found practice explained about 12% of the differences in performance overall, and under 1% in professions. Practice matters, but how you practise matters more than how long.
lesson: Hours aren't the point. Focused practice, with feedback, is.
check: Am I practising, or just repeating?
sources: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014). Deliberate Practice and Performance in Music, Games, Sports, Education, and Professions: A Meta-Analysis. Psychological Science 25(8)

keywords: how to get better at work
faq: Where does the 10,000-hour rule come from?
It was popularised by a 2008 bestselling book, based on a 1993 study by Anders Ericsson and colleagues of violinists.
Is the 10,000-hour rule true?

Not as a rule. In the original study, 10,000 hours was an average for the best violinists by age 20, not a threshold. A 2014 review of 88 studies found practice explained about 12% of differences in performance overall, and under 1% in professions.
What kind of practice works best?
Researchers point to deliberate practice: focused effort on specific weaknesses, with feedback, rather than simply repeating what you already do.

title: He failed 5,127 times. Then the experts said no.
summary: James Dyson built 5,127 prototypes of a bagless vacuum. The big manufacturers still turned it down, and their reason is the real lesson.
body: James Dyson wanted a vacuum cleaner that didn't need a bag. For about five years he built prototype after prototype in a shed behind his house, going deep into debt. Prototype number 5,127 finally worked.
Then the big vacuum makers said no. They earned a fortune selling replacement bags, and a bagless machine would have cut into that.
So Dyson licensed his design in Japan, and the royalties kept him going. In 1993 he launched his own machine in the UK. Within about 18 months it was the country's best-selling vacuum cleaner.
lesson: When experts say no, ask what they lose if you're right.

check: What would it cost them if I'm right?

How did Dyson succeed after being rejected?

title: She bet $5,000 on pantyhose. And kept her day job.
summary: Sara Blakely started Spanx with $5,000 of savings, no investors and her fax-machine sales job intact. Testing before quitting was the bold move.
body: Sara Blakely spent seven years selling fax machines door to door for the office supply company Danka, and was promoted to national sales trainer at 25. It was a steady job with a steady salary, and she kept it longer than most people would guess.

The idea came from a small problem. She wanted to wear white trousers without visible lines, so she cut the feet off a pair of control-top pantyhose and wore them underneath. It worked better than anything she could buy, and she saw a product.

She put about $5,000 of her own savings into it. She never took an outside investor; in her words, she started it "with five grand from selling fax machines." And she did not quit. For about two years she kept her job at Danka and worked on Spanx at night, researching fabrics and patents.

She only resigned after Oprah Winfrey picked Spanx as one of her "Favorite Things" in November 2000, a moment that helped drive sales. By 2012 Forbes put her on its cover as the youngest self-made female billionaire in the world.

In 2021, the investment firm Blackstone bought a majority stake in Spanx at a valuation of $1.2 billion, and Blakely stayed on as executive chairwoman. The famous part of the story is the billion. The useful part is the two years in between, when she tested the idea while her salary kept coming in. Forbes now estimates her net worth at about $1.3 billion.
lesson: The bold move wasn't quitting. It was testing first.
check_title: Before you bet your salary on an idea, ask:
check: What's the smallest test I could run while I still have my job?
What result would tell me it's time to jump?

Did Sara Blakely quit her job to start Spanx?
Not at first. She kept her job at the office supply company Danka for about two years and built Spanx at night, resigning only after Oprah named Spanx a Favorite Thing in November 2000.
How much was Spanx worth?
In 2021 Blackstone bought a majority stake in Spanx at a $1.2 billion valuation. In 2012 Forbes called Blakely the youngest self-made female billionaire in the world.

title: They could've bought Netflix for $50 million. Saying no made sense.
seo_title: Netflix's $50 million offer to Blockbuster: why it said no
summary: In 2000 Netflix offered itself to Blockbuster for $50 million. With what Blockbuster knew then, passing looked sensible. Here's what changed.
body: In 2000, Netflix co-founders Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph went to Blockbuster's offices in Texas to meet its CEO, John Antioco. Their offer was simple: buy Netflix for $50 million. Randolph later wrote that when the number was named, Antioco was "struggling not to laugh." Former Netflix CFO Barry McCarthy said Blockbuster "laughed us out of their office."

It is easy to mock that answer now, but look at what each side knew at the time. Blockbuster had about 9,000 locations at its peak and revenue in the $5 billion range. Netflix mailed DVDs to a small base of customers and was deep in losses; Hastings said the company was on track to lose at least $50 million that year. The dot-com bubble popped soon after. Paying $50 million for a money-losing website did not look clever.

Blockbuster did not ignore the internet either. It launched Blockbuster Online in 2004, and its 2006 Total Access plan, which let customers return mailed discs in stores, grew fast. In one quarter of 2007 Netflix lost 55,000 subscribers. Randolph has spoken about "how close Blockbuster came to actually winning."

What decided the race was less one meeting than what came after: leadership changes, pricing choices and debt. Hastings said in 2009, "If it hadn't been for their debt, they could have killed us." Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010. By 2020 Netflix had more than 183 million subscribers, after more than $20 billion of revenue in 2019.
The lesson is not that Blockbuster was foolish. It is that a small, struggling idea can still be pointing somewhere big, and that size today is a poor guide to where something is heading.
lesson: Don't judge an idea by its size today. Judge where it's heading.
check_title: Before you dismiss a small idea, ask:
check: If this keeps growing for five years, what does it become?
What would I have to believe for this to be worth far more than it looks?
keywords: Netflix offered to sell to Blockbuster
faq: Did Blockbuster really have the chance to buy Netflix?
Yes. In 2000 Netflix's co-founders Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph offered to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for $50 million, and Blockbuster's CEO John Antioco declined.
Why did Blockbuster say no to buying Netflix?

At the time Netflix was a small DVD-by-mail company expecting to lose at least $50 million that year, while Blockbuster had revenue of around $5 billion and thousands of stores, and the dot-com bubble was about to burst.
When did Blockbuster go bankrupt?
Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010. Netflix's Reed Hastings later said Blockbuster's debt was a key factor in the outcome.

title: This label said no to the Beatles. Then it learned.
seo_title: Why Decca rejected the Beatles in 1962, and what came next
summary: On 1 January 1962 Decca auditioned the Beatles and chose another band. A year later the same boss signed the Rolling Stones. Here's the story.
body: On Monday 1 January 1962, a young band from Liverpool arrived at Decca Studios in West Hampstead, London, for an audition. Starting at 11am and over roughly an hour, the Beatles recorded 15 songs under the supervision of Decca's A&R man Mike Smith. Their manager, Brian Epstein, hoped it would lead to a record deal.

It did not. Another group auditioned that same day: Brian Poole and the Tremeloes. Decca's head of A&R, Dick Rowe, and Mike Smith chose them, partly because they were based close to London. Rowe later explained, "We decided it was better to take the local group," because they could be worked with more easily.

The line everyone remembers comes from Epstein's 1964 autobiography, which quotes Rowe as saying, "Guitar groups are on their way out, Mr. Epstein." Rowe denied ever saying it. Either way, the Beatles kept going. Epstein had the Decca tapes copied, and they reached George Martin, head of A&R at Parlophone, part of EMI. Martin offered the band an audition at Abbey Road, and the band went on to sign with Parlophone.

Here is the part that is told less often. In May 1963, on a recommendation from George Harrison of the Beatles, Rowe went to see a new band at the Crawdaddy Club. Decca signed them within the week. They were the Rolling Stones.

So the label that passed on the Beatles did not repeat the mistake. A single miss, judged with what you knew at the time, is not the end of the story. Ignoring what it teaches you is what makes it expensive.
lesson: A miss only costs you twice if you ignore it.
check_title: After a decision goes wrong, ask:
check: What did I know at the time, and what would I look for differently next time?
Where is the next chance that looks like the one I missed?
keywords: guitar groups are on their way out
Brian Poole and the Tremeloes Decca
faq: Why did Decca reject the Beatles?
After the 1 January 1962 audition, Decca chose Brian Poole and the Tremeloes, who auditioned the same day, partly because they were based close to London and seen as easier to work with.
Who said "guitar groups are on their way out"?
Brian Epstein's 1964 autobiography attributes the line to Decca's head of A&R, Dick Rowe. Rowe denied ever saying it.
Did Decca sign the Rolling Stones?
Yes. In May 1963, on a recommendation from George Harrison, Dick Rowe saw the Rolling Stones and Decca signed them within the week.

title: He invented the digital camera. His company shelved it.
seo_title: Steve Sasson's 1975 digital camera: why Kodak held back
summary: In 1975 Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built the first digital camera. Kodak saw no market and kept it quiet. Here is what they knew at the time.
body: Steve Sasson joined Eastman Kodak in June 1973, fresh from a master's degree in electrical engineering at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. Working in Kodak's applied research laboratory, he built a camera around a new electronic image sensor, a CCD. By December 1975, at 24, he had a working camera that needed no film.

It was not pretty. The prototype was about the size of a toaster and weighed roughly 3.6 kilograms (about 8 pounds). Its Fairchild sensor captured a black-and-white image of just 100 by 100 pixels, or 0.01 megapixels. Taking the picture took 50 milliseconds, but recording it to a cassette tape took 23 seconds. To see the photo, you played the tape back on a television set.

Sasson demonstrated it to Kodak managers. He later described their reaction as "curiosity and skepticism", and said "they did not like the word 'digital'." He told the New York Times they were convinced that no one would ever want to look at their pictures on a television. Prints were cheap and familiar, and Kodak dominated the photo market through film. Sasson was not allowed to discuss the camera publicly or show it outside the company, though Kodak was granted a US patent for it in 1978.

Judged by what was known in 1975, the caution made sense: the camera was slow, heavy and needed a TV. But the technology kept improving. Kodak launched its own digital camera about 18 years later, by which time the shift was well under way. In 2012 Eastman Kodak filed for bankruptcy, and it emerged in 2013.
Sasson's work was eventually celebrated. He received the US National Medal of Technology and Innovation in 2009, and the IEEE commemorated his camera as a Milestone.
lesson: If a new idea threatens your best seller, someone else will build it. Better to learn from it early than to be surprised by it later.
check_title: Before you dismiss a clumsy new idea, ask:
check: Am I judging it by how good it is today, or by how fast it is improving?
Am I saying no because it is weak, or because it threatens something I already earn from?
keywords: why Kodak shelved the digital camera
faq: Who invented the first digital camera?
Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built the first self-contained portable digital camera in 1975, working in Kodak's applied research laboratory.
Why didn't Kodak sell the digital camera in 1975?
Executives didn't see a market: the prototype weighed about 8 pounds, took 23 seconds to save each photo and needed a TV to view it, and Kodak's business was built on film.
How many pixels did the first digital camera have?
It captured black-and-white images of 100 by 100 pixels, or 10,000 pixels (0.01 megapixels), recorded onto cassette tape.

title: His game flopped. Its chat tool sold for $27.7 billion.
seo_title: Slack's origin story: how a failed game became $27.7B
summary: Stewart Butterfield's online game Glitch shut down in 2012. The chat tool his team built to make it became Slack, sold to Salesforce for $27.7 billion.
body: In 2009 Stewart Butterfield, already known as a co-founder of Flickr, co-founded a company called Tiny Speck. Its first product was Glitch, a quirky online game with hand-drawn 2D worlds. Glitch launched on 27 September 2011.

The game struggled from the start. Within two months the team pulled it back to improve the gameplay, and in November 2012 Tiny Speck announced that Glitch would close. The game world shut down on 9 December 2012.

But while building Glitch, the team had made something for themselves: an internal chat tool to talk to each other. After the game closed, Butterfield turned that tool into the company's product. He announced Slack in August 2013 and it became publicly available in February 2014. The name stood for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge". The company raised $17 million from investors including Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, and in August 2014 renamed itself Slack Technologies.

Slack grew quickly: its revenue rose from $105.2 million in 2017 to $400.6 million in the fiscal year ending January 2019. It listed on the stock market in June 2019, and on 1 December 2020 Salesforce announced it would buy Slack for $27.7 billion. The deal closed on 21 July 2021.

It was not the first time this happened to Butterfield. In 2002 he co-founded Ludicorp to build an online game called Game Neverending. The game never launched, but tools built for it grew into Flickr, which went live in February 2004 and was bought by Yahoo in March 2005. Twice, the side tool turned out to be the real business.
lesson: The tool you built to solve your own problem might be worth more than the project it was built for. When a plan fails, look at what you made along the way.
check_title: Before you write off a project that didn't work, ask:
check: What did we build for ourselves that others might need too?
Am I attached to the original plan, or to solving a real problem?
keywords: how Slack started from a failed game
faq: How did Slack start?

Slack began as an internal chat tool that Stewart Butterfield's team at Tiny Speck built while making the online game Glitch. After Glitch closed in December 2012, they turned the tool into a product, released publicly in February 2014.
How much did Salesforce pay for Slack?
Salesforce announced on 1 December 2020 that it would buy Slack for $27.7 billion. The acquisition was completed on 21 July 2021.
Did Flickr also come from a game?
Yes. Flickr grew out of tools built for Game Neverending, an online game from Butterfield's company Ludicorp that never launched. Flickr went live in February 2004 and Yahoo bought it in March 2005.

title: He started over at 65. On $105 a month.
seo_title: Colonel Sanders started over at 65: the KFC story
summary: A new interstate emptied Harland Sanders's Kentucky cafe. At 65 he sold it at a loss, hit the road with his chicken recipe and built KFC.
body: Harland Sanders was born in 1890 in Henryville, Indiana. By the 1940s he was running the Sanders Cafe in Corbin, Kentucky, a roadside restaurant beside a busy highway that became known for his fried chicken. In 1935 Kentucky's governor had made him an honorary Kentucky colonel, the title he kept for the rest of his life.

In 1952 he licensed his chicken recipe to Pete Harman, who ran a restaurant in Salt Lake City. Harman became the first Kentucky Fried Chicken franchisee. But Sanders's own income still depended on the cafe in Corbin, and on the traffic that drove past it.

In 1956 a new stretch of Interstate 75 opened and bypassed the town. Customer numbers plummeted. At 65, Sanders was forced to sell the cafe, and the auction brought far less than it was worth. He was left with his savings and a Social Security check of $105 a month.

Instead of retiring, he went on the road with his recipe, visiting restaurants and selling them the right to serve his chicken. It worked: by 1964 Kentucky Fried Chicken had more than 600 franchised outlets in the United States and Canada.

That year, Sanders sold the company to a group of investors led by John Y. Brown Jr. and Jack Massey for $2 million in cash, plus a salary to stay on as the brand's ambassador, a role he kept for life. By 1980 the chain's stores were reporting more than $2 billion in sales a year.
lesson: Losing the plan you built is not the same as losing what you are good at. Sanders's cafe was gone, but his recipe and his skill at selling it were not, and those turned out to be the real business.
check_title: If your current plan stopped working tomorrow, ask:
check: What am I great at that other people would pay for?
Who could I sell it to this month, not someday?
keywords: never too late to start a business
faq: How old was Colonel Sanders when he started KFC?

Sanders licensed his recipe to his first franchisee, Pete Harman, in 1952. He turned franchising into his full-time work after he was forced to sell his Corbin, Kentucky cafe at 65, when a new interstate bypassed it in 1956.
How much was Colonel Sanders's Social Security check?
After selling his cafe at a loss, Sanders lived on a Social Security check of $105 a month while he travelled to sell his recipe to restaurants.
How much did Colonel Sanders sell KFC for?
In 1964, with more than 600 outlets, Sanders sold Kentucky Fried Chicken to investors led by John Y. Brown Jr. and Jack Massey for $2 million, plus a salary to stay on as its ambassador.
